title: They Dedicated Their Lives to Teaching. Then the Deepfakes Started
gist: Four educators describe students generating and circulating sexualized AI images and impersonation accounts of them on TikTok and Snapchat, with school discipline capping out at three-day suspensions and platforms responding inconsistently. The reporting exposes a governance vacuum: the federal Take It Down Act may apply, employers owe a harassment-free workplace, but there is no blueprint for how schools must respond.

insights.claim: A substitute teacher in Los Banos, California found an AI-altered version of his own college mirror selfie circulating on TikTok, showing him in lingerie and posing suggestively, traced to students at the middle school where he regularly filled in.
insights.so_what: Source material is ordinary public photos — meaning any employee with an online image footprint is exposed, not just public figures.
insights.quote: Parts of it resembled a mirror selfie that he remembered taking at a job in college. But instead of his work uniform, he was wearing lingerie.
insights.locator: “When I finally saw the image, that’s when it felt like a punch to the gut,”
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: WIRED spoke with four educators in total who allege students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI, indicating the pattern is not isolated to one school or country.
insights.so_what: A recurring pattern across US and UK schools points to a systemic content-moderation and school-policy gap, not anecdote.
insights.quote: WIRED spoke with three other teachers who allege that their students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI.
insights.locator: The texts kicked off a monthslong saga
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Impersonation accounts compound the image problem: one student created a TikTok account using the substitute teacher's slightly misspelled name and his photo as the profile picture.
insights.so_what: Identity impersonation and synthetic imagery are one combined attack surface; platform name-squatting controls are the weak link.
insights.quote: He discovered that a different student had created an account impersonating him—it used his name, slightly mispelled, and had the same photo as their profile picture.
insights.locator: Later that evening, he decided to look for the image
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Synthetic video impersonation is already convincing enough that students believed a fake TikTok account was genuinely their teacher discussing sexual acts, despite visible AI tells like unnatural mouth movement and a mismatched voice.
insights.so_what: Detection tells exist but audiences ignore them; reputational damage lands before any takedown, which is what makes the harm economically real.
insights.quote: “I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me genuinely believed that was my account, and that I was saying those things,”
insights.locator: “I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Once created, the images propagate across multiple platforms and channels — TikTok, Snapchat, AirDrop and group chats — so a single takedown does not end the exposure.
insights.so_what: Per-platform moderation is structurally insufficient against peer-to-peer redistribution; the moderation problem is a network problem.
insights.quote: During one class, he received an AirDropped photo of the same AI-generated image before it was quickly revoked.
insights.locator: He took a substitute assignment at the local high school
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Disseminating fake nude images of nonconsenting adults may constitute cyberstalking and violate the federal Take It Down Act, which criminalizes publishing nonconsensual intimate visual depictions that are either authentic or computer-generated.
insights.so_what: US law already reaches synthetic imagery explicitly; platform compliance obligations here are the near-term enforcement risk.
insights.quote: the federal Take It Down Act, which makes it a crime to publish nonconsensual “intimate visual depictions of individuals, both authentic and computer-generated,” on the internet
insights.locator: When fake nude images of nonconsenting adults are disseminated
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: A retired employment lawyer argues that a student creating and sharing sexual images of a teacher is a clear case of workplace sexual harassment, triggering employers' federal antidiscrimination obligation to maintain a harassment-free workplace.
insights.so_what: Reframes deepfakes as an employer-liability problem, not just a platform problem — school districts and any employer carry direct exposure.
insights.quote: constitutes a “clear case” of sexual harassment in the workplace
insights.locator: Donna Ballman, a retired employment advocacy lawyer
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: There is no blueprint for how schools must respond to AI harassment incidents, and administrators are not even required to tell a victimized teacher how the offending student was disciplined — only to create a safe environment.
insights.so_what: Procedural vacuum means outcomes vary wildly by district, which is precisely the condition that produces litigation and eventual statutory mandates.
insights.quote: there's “no blueprint” for how schools need to respond to these incidents. Administrators don’t even have to tell a victimized teacher how a student may have been disciplined.
insights.locator: Ballman says that under federal antidiscrimination laws
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: In most accounts shared with WIRED the teachers did not directly report the content to the platforms it appeared on, meaning platform-side reporting metrics systematically understate the incidence of this harm.
insights.so_what: Any platform-reported prevalence numbers on AI sexual harassment should be treated as a floor, not an estimate.
insights.quote: In most of the accounts shared with WIRED, the teachers didn't directly report the content to the platforms on which it appeared.
insights.locator: In most of the accounts shared with WIRED
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

themes.theme: Weak enforcement at platform and district level

insights.claim: Discipline for a first-time sexual harassment offense involving AI imagery topped out at a three-day suspension in one Arizona district — the most severe punishment available for that age group under the district handbook.
insights.so_what: Sanction ceilings this low mean deterrence has to come from platforms or statute, not from schools.
insights.quote: The student received a three-day suspension—the most severe punishment kids their age can receive for a first-time sexual harassment offense, according to the school district handbook.
insights.locator: Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: TikTok declined to remove accounts an Arizona teacher reported for being under the minimum age of 13, showing age-based enforcement failing even when the reporting user identifies the violation category.
insights.so_what: Underage-account enforcement is a live regulatory target; documented non-removal on direct report is the evidence regulators use.
insights.quote: Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok—not for content violations but for being under the minimum age of 13—but says TikTok didn’t remove the accounts.
insights.locator: Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Snap points to existing policies prohibiting AI-generated or manipulated content used to humiliate or sexually harass, and to established reporting processes; TikTok did not provide comment before publication.
insights.so_what: Policy-on-paper versus enforcement-in-practice is the gap; differential responsiveness between Snap and TikTok is itself a signal on regulatory exposure.
insights.locator: Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy shared the company's policies
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: Synthetic-image incidents escalated into sustained in-person harassment in one case, with the same student cursing at the teacher, calling and texting an assistant principal in the middle of the night, and posting AI photos of them — ending only when the student left the district.
insights.so_what: AI content is an escalation vector into physical-world harassment, which raises the duty-of-care stakes for institutions well beyond content removal.
insights.quote: “cursing me out, calling me names, telling me to fuck off, calling me a bitch.”
insights.locator: As days and weeks passed, she says, she became the target
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

themes.theme: Second-order effects on the teaching workforce

insights.claim: The substitute teacher told administrators he would not take assignments at the middle school until the matter was addressed and says he probably won't return to the district this year because he does not feel safe.
insights.so_what: AI harassment translates directly into staffing attrition in an already thin substitute-teacher labor market.
insights.locator: DeSantiago told administrators he didn’t want to take assignments
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: A UK college counselor who meets individually with about 150 students a year says a deepfake incident made her reassess her mentoring conversations and left the classroom atmosphere chilled even after she returned.
insights.so_what: The damage is to the trust infrastructure of the job itself — a cost that does not show up in takedown statistics.
insights.quote: “It makes me reflect as well on those conversations, thinking, did he think that he could overstep a line because we were having these discussions?”
insights.locator: “It makes me reflect as well on those conversations
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: One victimized teacher's principal concern is not the image itself but the permissive culture around AI use among students, where kids felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images in the first place.
insights.so_what: Norm formation, not tooling access, is identified as the root variable — implying education and product friction matter more than model-level guardrails alone.
insights.quote: “It just got to the point where students felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images,”
insights.locator: “It just got to the point where students felt comfortable
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins

insights.claim: A teacher who reported an incident warned administrators that if students are willing to post such images publicly, they are likely circulating material privately through text messages and group chats — potentially including images of other students.
insights.so_what: The visible incidents are a sampling of a larger private-channel volume; child-safety exposure is the tail risk platforms and districts are not measuring.
